query: The Lamplighter's Round {At dusk the old porter makes his round with a long brass pole, lighting the corridor lamps one by one. He's slow these days, and the west corridor is long.|The lamplighter again, at dusk. He nods at the spare pole leaning by the door, as if it had been left there for someone.|The lamplighter's round. The spare pole has a notch carved in it now, about where your hand goes.} {He hums an old song as he goes.|His knees click on every stair.|{season == "winter": It's been dark for an hour already, and every lamp matters.|The evening is long and gold, and he's in no hurry.}} Light the west corridor for him {You light them with a flick of fire, one after another, all the way to the end, and feel each one in your fingertips. The porter says the corridor has never looked so cheerful, and he's been doing it forty years.|You take the far end with the spare pole and a little flame. He takes the near end and tells you about the castle when he was a boy. You're drained, and lit up.|You light the west corridor in a single walk now, a flame at every lamp, and you're light-headed by the end. The porter lights his pipe off the last one.} Walk with him and listen {He tells you which lamps never stay lit and why, and which ghost likes the dark. You walk the whole round and forget you had anywhere to be.|He tells you about a headmistress, long ago, who lit every lamp in the castle with one snap of her fingers. "Showing off," he says fondly.|He tells you a story for every lamp. You've heard some before. You don't mind.}
